Where I stopped
I hit the tool-use limit mid-build. Rather than hand you a half-finished archive, here's exactly what I found, what I decided, and what's written so far — so the next turn can produce the complete .tar.gz without re-deriving anything.

State of the tree (from dump.txt + claude-terminal.txt)
Your last sweep is green: dotnet build clean, dotnet test = 470 total, 0 failed, 455 passed, 15 skipped (the M6 Playwright matrix), run.sh --smoke passed, containers up, quick tunnel up. The /account/enroll-totp 500 is fixed (the static-SSR intermediate-render _start! deref — else → else if (_start is not null)).

BUILD_PROGRESS.md shows M3 Slices 1–3 landed. The next slice it names is: display pairing, device auth, and /display/{table} (§4.2, §11.5, §3.7).

Design decisions I locked in (all verified against dotnet/aspnetcore release/10.0)
Device principal via plain middleware, not an auth scheme. A custom AuthenticationHandler would break the interactive circuit: /_blazor authenticates with the default scheme, so CircuitHost would capture an anonymous principal. A middleware after UseAuthentication() scoped to /display* and /_blazor sets HttpContext.User, which flows to the circuit correctly.
/display/{table} is anonymous at the endpoint, device-gated in-page. §11.5 says an unpaired device redirects to /display/pair — a policy challenge would send it to /sign-in. The table-claim match is a route-value comparison anyway, exactly like /table's per-sitting membership check that §3.7 already leaves outside the policy.
No role claim for table_display — a myrestaurant:principal_kind claim instead, so RequireRole can never match a device.
Rate limiting — confirmed @attribute [EnableRateLimiting(...)] works: RazorComponentEndpointFactory says "All attributes defined for the type are included as metadata", and RateLimitingMiddleware reads endpoint.Metadata.GetMetadata<EnableRateLimitingAttribute>(). RateLimitPartition.GetFixedWindowLimiter + FixedWindowRateLimiterOptions confirmed in System.Threading.RateLimiting ref for .NET 10. Partitioned on Connection.RemoteIpAddress, so UseRateLimiter() must sit after UseForwardedHeaders().
Staleness indicator without framework internals — data-refresh-token + data-fresh-for-ms on the surface, and display.js records when it observes a token change. Immune to kiosk clock skew; if the circuit dies the attribute stops changing and the overlay appears.
InputSelect bound to string, not Guid — avoids any BindConverter risk; matches the ManagePerson.razor select pattern already in the tree.
Revoke uses one select-driven form, not per-row forms — same reason.

M3 Slice 4 — display devices: pairing, device authentication, and the /display surfaces. 24 files, extracts at the repo root.

bash
cd /home/kushal/src/dotnet/myrestaurant
tar -xzf ~/Downloads/m3-slice4-display-devices.tar.gz
cat docs/BUILD_PROGRESS.append.md >> docs/BUILD_PROGRESS.md && rm docs/BUILD_PROGRESS.append.md
Files to delete: none. No migration (both display tables ship in 0001), no packages (rate limiting is in the shared framework), no spec/ADR edit — this realizes §4.2, §3.7, and §11.5 as written.

Two things worth knowing before you read the diff
The device principal is middleware, not an auth scheme. A custom AuthenticationHandler is the obvious shape and it silently breaks the display: /display/{table} is interactive, and a circuit takes its principal from the /_blazor request, which authenticates with the default scheme. A device scheme would populate the initial GET and hand the circuit an anonymous principal. Middleware runs on both.

/display/{table} is anonymous at the endpoint, gated in the component. §11.5 requires an unpaired device to be redirected to /display/pair; [Authorize] can't do that — a failed policy challenges the default scheme and lands a tablet on /sign-in.

One pre-existing issue I found while verifying
I checked EditForm in release/10.0: RenderSSRFormHandlingChildren already opens an AntiforgeryToken component for any named SSR form. So an explicit <AntiforgeryToken /> inside an EditForm renders a second hidden field of the same name, and DefaultAntiforgeryTokenStore casts form[fieldName] to string? — which yields null for multi-valued StringValues, i.e. "the required antiforgery field is not present."

ManagePerson.razor has that duplicate on both manage-grant-role and manage-revoke-role. ManageTable.razor's rename form doesn't, and you've exercised that one. So the role grant/revoke forms may be latently broken in a way no unit test would catch. Worth clicking through once. I've followed the ManageTable pattern in my own pages: no explicit token inside EditForm, explicit token on plain <form> elements.

Highest-risk file for the compiler
Components/Pages/Display/TableDisplay.razor — the first interactive component here with a background refresh loop, a broadcaster subscription, and IDisposable. If anything catches, it'll be there.

The manual checklist is at the end of the appended BUILD_PROGRESS section; the short version is: generate a code, pair a second browser profile, watch the QR change across a boundary, join from a phone and see the chip move, then podman-compose --profile dev stop web and confirm the red Reconnecting… curtain drops within about 70 seconds.
